title: Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source

concept.text: The innovation would be a source that produces spatially coherent hard X-rays inside an ordinary laboratory, with enough usable radiation to perform substantive imaging or spectroscopy. Spatial coherence describes the relationship between the radiation across its wavefront, a property needed for interference-based measurements and coherent imaging. The target combines photon energy, coherence, usable photon delivery and a practical installation footprint; producing hard X-rays or shrinking an accelerator alone would establish only part of it. The supplied 2021 research documents compact X-ray free-electron lasers as a prospective goal, rather than demonstrating this combined capability.

Conceptual synthesis: the innovation is defined by source performance rather than by a single generation mechanism. High-harmonic generation, laser-wakefield-driven free-electron lasers and high-gain inverse Compton schemes are candidate routes discussed in the supplied research. Each would have to deliver coherent radiation at several keV or higher, sufficient photons within the experiment's accepted spectrum, and stable operation in a documented laboratory installation. The proposed energy and operating requirements describe the intended target; their combined feasibility is not established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: A successful source could bring some coherent hard X-ray experiments into individual laboratories, expanding local access and opportunities for repeated measurements and instrument development. The 2021 Nature abstract motivates compact accelerators by describing the large, costly radio-frequency accelerators used by operating XFEL facilities and identifies coherent XFEL radiation as important to structural biology, chemistry and other disciplines. This supports the access-related significance without establishing that all coherent hard X-ray work is restricted to national facilities or follows a particular beamtime allocation process.

Impact synthesis: comparison with the optical laser is useful specifically as an analogy about making a scientifically valuable form of coherent radiation locally available. It is not a prediction that a laboratory hard X-ray source would reproduce the optical laser's historical effects, costs or range of uses. The practical transformation would depend on how many experiments the source could support, how reliably it operated and how demanding its installation and maintenance were.

Application synthesis: potential uses include element-specific imaging, lensless microscopy and spectroscopy, but each requires a suitable combination of spectrum, spatial coherence and detected signal. Ultrafast diffraction would additionally require demonstrated pulse duration, synchronization and adequate photons per pulse. Kilohertz operation and useful average flux would not by themselves establish those temporal capabilities. Lithography-scale extreme-ultraviolet power and replacement of the full range of XFEL experiments would remain separate advances, with different requirements for wavelength, average power, brightness and experimental performance.

The temporal distinction matters to the historical evidence as well. In the associated 2021 peer-review file, the authors stated that their experimental system did not yet permit an exact radiation bunch-length measurement. Their reported pulse energy therefore does not independently demonstrate the pulse duration needed for an ultrafast application.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is the integration of coherent hard X-ray generation, application-level photon delivery and practical laboratory operation. A documented historical step toward that goal was the 2021 demonstration of laser-wakefield-driven exponential free-electron gain at typically 27 nm. Its associated peer-review correspondence described higher gain, saturation and extension to X-ray wavelengths as future objectives. That establishes the challenge as understood in 2021; it cannot establish whether those objectives remained unmet on 1 November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: for a compact free-electron-laser route, the challenge is to produce an electron beam whose energy, brightness, energy spread and stability permit sustained amplification at the desired hard X-ray wavelength, and to preserve the necessary beam quality through transport and interaction with the radiation-generating structure. Acceleration, beam transport, gain and repeatability must work together. The laser-wakefield demonstration means it would be inaccurate to claim that every instance of free-electron lasing requires a conventional large accelerator.

Engineering synthesis: for a high-harmonic route, reaching a high photon-energy cutoff is only one requirement. A practical source must also maintain coherent generation and deliver sufficient photons in the bandwidth accepted by the experiment. Driver efficiency, phase matching, absorption, optical losses, heat removal and stable operation at the intended repetition rate would need to be assessed together. These are proposed barrier categories, not verified quantitative limits extracted from the uncaptured Science paper.

Engineering synthesis: all routes also face the difference between generating radiation and delivering a useful measurement. Collection optics, spectral selection, sample illumination and detector efficiency determine how many generated photons contribute to the result. The footprint must include the driver laser or accelerator, supporting equipment, shielding and operational infrastructure. The supplied material does not establish a specific electron-brightness or laser-energy feasibility boundary for inverse Compton sources, because the cited 2025 analysis was not captured.

current_state.text: Wang, Feng, Ke and colleagues reported a laser-wakefield-driven free-electron-laser experiment in Nature in July 2021. The retained abstract supports undulator-radiation amplification in the exponential-gain regime at typically 27 nm, with a maximum photon number around 10¹⁰ per shot and maximum radiation energy about 150 nJ. The photon count and energy are reported maxima, not average output or typical shot performance; the supplied review does not establish that both maxima occurred on the same shot. This is an important compact-accelerator gain demonstration, but it does not demonstrate the proposed laboratory hard X-ray source.

Access to that result was partial in the supplied review. The retained Nature page is a subscription preview containing the abstract. The substantial retained PDF is the associated peer-review file, rather than the research article itself. It documents author responses, additional measurements and analysis, and later reviewer acceptance; initial objections should therefore be interpreted alongside their subsequent resolution, rather than treated as evidence that the published gain result was rejected. Two other retained PDFs contain only minimally extracted plot text, lack enough identifying text for confident interpretation and were not visually inspected. They do not supply an independent full-article verification.

The supplied research attributes to Popmintchev and colleagues a Science result dated 8 June 2012: a spatially coherent supercontinuum extending beyond 1.6 keV and above the 5000th harmonic, generated through phase-matched high-harmonic generation with a mid-infrared driver. These specifications are preserved here as an account from the research notes. No artifact of the cited Science paper was available in the supplied review, so its spectrum, coherence characterization and experimental conditions could not be verified from the retained evidence. The missing artifact does not show that the result is false.

The research also attributes an output of about 10⁸ photons per second in a 1 percent bandwidth near 1 keV to an Oxford Instruments application note describing that experiment, with an update date of 16 July 2025. This is a secondary-source estimate, separate from the Science paper. The retained Oxford material consists only of a heading about a tabletop coherent X-ray source in the keV region. It cannot verify the experimental attribution, numerical flux, bandwidth or update date. The estimate should consequently remain attributed and unverified, rather than being used as an established performance benchmark.

The research notes describe a 2025 Optica analysis of high-gain inverse Compton sources, dated 4 March 2025, as finding hard X-rays beyond near-term electron-brightness and laser-energy capabilities. No artifact of that source was supplied. Its assumptions, quantitative bounds and conclusion therefore cannot be verified here, and the earlier assertion that page details had been obtained from retrieved full text is not retained. This remains an attributed account of an analysis, rather than a demonstrated source result or an established exclusion of the approach.

Evidence-bound synthesis: the supplied record does not establish whether a laboratory source meeting the combined hard X-ray, coherence, flux and operational requirements had been demonstrated by 1 November 2026. The bounded search record is empty, so freshness was not assessed. The appropriate conclusion is that the documented 2021 gain experiment is a partial advance toward the target, while the target's present achievement remains unresolved in this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a source in an explicitly documented ordinary-laboratory installation, producing spatially coherent radiation at several keV or higher at a measured kilohertz-class repetition rate. Report the complete footprint and supporting infrastructure, including the driver, radiation-producing beamline, shielding and utilities. Several keV, kilohertz operation and an ordinary-laboratory footprint are proposed choices for evaluating this innovation, not agency requirements or established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Ordinary-laboratory source delivers spatially coherent kilohertz-class X-rays at several keV

completion_criteria.text: Proposed source characterization: measure photon energy, spectrum and bandwidth, spatial coherence, delivered photon flux, photons per pulse, shot-to-shot variation and stability over a stated operating period. Distinguish peak or maximum performance from typical and sustained performance, and state whether the advertised properties were obtained simultaneously. A source should meet the combined target in an identified operating configuration rather than assemble its specification from incompatible settings.
completion_criteria.label: Source characterization reports simultaneous performance in an identified operating configuration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed application demonstration: publish an imaging or spectroscopy measurement representative of work performed at a synchrotron or XFEL, with an explicit account of the measurement's requirements. Report detected photons, acquisition time, resolution or sensitivity, sample conditions, background and uncertainty, so that readers can assess what the laboratory source actually enables. Publication would make the result assessable; it would not substitute for measured performance. Any claim to ultrafast diffraction should additionally report pulse duration, timing synchronization and the per-pulse signal relevant to that experiment.
completion_criteria.label: Published imaging or spectroscopy quantifies performance against synchrotron or XFEL requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the performance across multiple runs and demonstrate either independent replication or sufficiently detailed methods and calibration for others to reproduce it. Report uptime, alignment demands, maintenance, operating costs and restrictions on samples or measurement modes. If a free-electron-laser implementation claims saturation, demonstrate saturation separately from exponential gain. Successful finite tests would establish the demonstrated range of applications and operating conditions; they would not establish universal replacement of synchrotrons or XFELs.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated source performance is reproducible, with practical operating boundaries reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, and OPT-02, Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold, share an interest in controlled light generation or manipulation. Their titles identify distinct targets involving optical switching and deterministic single-photon delivery. OPT-04 instead concerns coherent hard X-ray radiation with sufficient aggregate usable flux for scientific measurements. Neither a few-photon switching demonstration nor an array of single-photon sources establishes this source capability.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-03, Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow, also concerns making coherent sources practical in a new setting. Its defining requirements concern electrical pumping and integration into a silicon manufacturing process. OPT-04 is defined by hard X-ray photon energy, coherence, experimental utility and laboratory footprint; it does not require CMOS integration. OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages, concerns efficient information transfer within packages rather than hard X-ray generation.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-05, Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue, and OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic, overlap with OPT-04 through imaging ambitions, but address different physical limitations. A useful hard X-ray source would not by itself establish cellular imaging through living tissue at video rates or a visible-light super-resolution optic. Each would still require its own imaging mechanism, sample compatibility and demonstrated resolution and acquisition performance.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-07, Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture, concerns control of a visible optical field across an aperture. It shares the broader importance of wavefront properties with coherent X-ray work, but the roster does not establish that its materials or control methods transfer to hard X-rays. OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium, concerns a distinct nonlinear interaction target; a compact coherent hard X-ray source would not on its own demonstrate that interaction.

Roster-based synthesis: OPT-10, Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras, concerns detection in a different spectral range. OPT-04's practical value also depends on detection, but a short-wave-infrared camera would not demonstrate a suitable hard X-ray detector. Across the roster, OPT-04 sits primarily in coherent radiation generation and source engineering, with substantial overlap in accelerator and plasma physics and potential applications in materials science, chemistry and structural biology. These relationships preserve all supplied concepts as separate targets.

unresolved_issues: Whether any source met the combined laboratory footprint, spatial coherence, hard X-ray energy, repetition-rate and application-flux target by 1 November 2026 remains unassessed.
The 2012 Science result's exact spectrum, harmonic order, coherence measurements and experimental conditions require verification from the missing source.
The Oxford note's experimental attribution, approximately 10⁸ photons per second estimate, 1 percent bandwidth and stated update date remain unverified.
The 2025 Optica analysis's identity details, assumptions, numerical bounds and conclusion cannot be confirmed from the supplied record.
The full 2021 Nature research article was not available in the retained material; the abstract and peer-review file support only the scope described here.

An ordinary-laboratory footprint, reference application, required signal quality and acceptable operating burden still need concrete definitions. The proposed several-keV and kilohertz criteria are not established standards.
Ultrafast performance would require separate temporal measurements; it cannot be inferred from spatial coherence, pulse energy or repetition rate.

brief.title: Powerful X-ray imaging in ordinary laboratories
possible: Researchers could make detailed images and study materials with powerful X-rays in their own laboratories. The source would produce hard X-rays, a high-energy form, with spatial coherence: a consistent relationship between waves across the beam.
why: Local access could let researchers repeat measurements more readily and develop new instruments. Structural biology and chemistry could benefit from bringing some experiments into individual laboratories.

sources.showed: This is an experimental study of coherent X-ray generation by converting laser light to higher photon energies.
sources.cited_for: It supports laser-based generation as a route toward a laboratory source.
sources.not_established: Reaching high photon energies does not establish enough usable radiation for practical hard X-ray experiments.

sources.showed: This is an application note describing a tabletop coherent X-ray experiment and estimating its photon output.
sources.cited_for: It discusses the usable output of a laser-based coherent X-ray source.
sources.not_established: An output estimate does not demonstrate the combined energy, coherence, stability and laboratory operation required.

sources.who: Wentao Wang, Ke Feng, Lintong Ke and colleagues
sources.showed: They used electrons from a compact laser-driven accelerator to amplify radiation. Its typical wavelength, the distance between wave peaks, was 27 nanometres.
sources.quote: Here we present an experimental demonstration of undulator radiation amplification in the exponential-gain regime by using electron beams based on a laser wakefield accelerator.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates radiation amplification driven by a compact accelerator.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate a laboratory source delivering coherent hard X-rays for useful measurements.

sources.who: The authors of the proposed X-ray source analysis
sources.showed: This is a feasibility analysis of a proposed method for amplifying X-rays.
sources.cited_for: It examines whether electron-beam quality and laser energy could support a proposed hard X-ray source.
sources.not_established: A feasibility analysis does not demonstrate a working source or rule out every implementation.

shown: Wang, Feng, Ke and colleagues demonstrated radiation amplification using a compact laser-driven accelerator. Popmintchev and colleagues reported coherent radiation extending beyond 1.6 kiloelectronvolts, a measure of photon energy. These are separate steps toward the combined capability.
missing: A source must combine hard X-ray energy, spatial coherence and enough delivered photons for a useful laboratory measurement.
All advertised properties must work together in the same operating setup.
Repeated experiments must establish reliability and the full demands of installation, maintenance and operation.

milestones.label: Coherent hard X-rays operate in an ordinary laboratory
milestones.explanation: A source would have to produce spatially coherent hard X-rays at roughly a thousand pulses per second, with all supporting equipment documented. This would establish the energy, repetition rate and installation requirements together.

milestones.label: All source properties are measured together
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to establish energy, spectral range, coherence, delivered photon output and stability in the same setup. This would show that useful performance persists beyond isolated best shots.

milestones.label: A published measurement demonstrates useful imaging or material analysis
milestones.explanation: A published experiment would have to quantify image quality or sensitivity against requirements for work at a major X-ray facility. This would establish a useful application; ultrafast claims would also require pulse and timing measurements.

milestones.label: Repeated performance establishes reproducibility and operating limits
milestones.explanation: Repeated runs would have to establish reproducibility, with independent replication or adequate methods, and report operating burdens. This would define practical use; claims that amplification reaches its limit would need separate demonstration.

uncertain: Whether any source has achieved the combined capability remains unresolved.
What counts as an ordinary laboratory, adequate signal quality and an acceptable operating burden still needs concrete definitions.
Spatial coherence and pulse energy alone do not establish whether a source can capture ultrafast changes.

page.title: Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source
page.definition: An installation that fits in a university laboratory delivers spatially coherent hard X-rays, of photon energy at least 5 keV, with enough coherent flux for the diffraction imaging now done at synchrotron beamlines. Spatial coherence is phase correlation across the beam; coherent flux is the photons per second within the coherent part of the beam.

goal.need: Photon delivery limits laboratory coherent imaging: the Sheffield proof of concept required 140 s exposures at each scan position, and its reconstruction remained photon-limited.

figures.caption: Photon delivery in the Sheffield laboratory demonstration
figures.note: The flux measurement includes the radiation transmitted through the pinhole; it is not a measurement of the source's coherent fraction.

statements.body: Diamond Light Source, Imaging and Microscopy Group
statements.quote: We have been leading developments in ptychography to open this technique to new science areas and communities.
statements.context: Statement by group leader Paul Quinn accompanying the laboratory demonstration.

statements.quote: we propose here a new class of UC-XFEL sources that can be implemented at the university level
statements.context: UC-XFEL means ultra-compact X-ray free-electron laser. The study includes soft- and hard-X-ray designs, a more demanding capability than the minimum imaging benchmark below.

completion.title: A laboratory-footprint source delivers 10⁸ coherent hard X-ray photons per second and a coherent image.
completion.criterion: One installation no longer than 50 m, including its driver, radiation source and shielding, delivers to a sample spatially coherent X-rays of photon energy at least 5 keV with measured coherent flux of at least 10⁸ photons s⁻¹, at a pulse rate of at least 1 kHz or continuously. Photon energy, bandwidth, coherence, flux and pulse rate are measured in one operating configuration, and the footprint is reported. A coherent diffraction measurement made with that beam, such as far-field ptychography, is reconstructed. The results are published after peer review. Any mechanism counts: free-electron laser, inverse Compton scattering, high-harmonic generation or electron impact.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas. The 50 m footprint is the UC-XFEL collaboration's design figure for a university-scale X-ray laser; the 5 keV, 10⁸ photons s⁻¹ and 1 kHz figures are the Atlas's.
completion.threshold_quote: the total longitudinal footprint of the instrument is below 50 m
completion.basis: No agency, programme or standard states a combined footprint, coherence and flux test; DARPA AXiS, NSF CXFEL and UC-XFEL documents were searched. The entry asks for flux sufficient for synchrotron-type measurements. The first laboratory ptychography had about 5 × 10³ photons s⁻¹ through its pinhole and 140 s per scan position, about 7 × 10⁵ photons; at 10⁸ photons s⁻¹ that exposure takes 7 ms and the 400-position scan about 3 s in place of 16 h. 5 keV is a common lower bound for hard X-rays; 1 kHz is the repetition class the entry names.

milestones.title: A laboratory X-ray source produces propagation-based hard X-ray phase contrast.
milestones.criterion: Produce phase-contrast images using spatially coherent hard X-rays and free-space propagation. Wilkins and colleagues demonstrated a scheme compatible with polychromatic microfocus X-ray tubes, published 28 November 1996. The accessible abstract supplies no numerical coherence or contrast cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Phase-contrast imaging community; the physical demonstration used by CSIRO's Wilkins and colleagues in their 1996 Nature paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: Here we describe and demonstrate a simplified scheme for phase-contrast imaging based on an X-ray source having high spatial (but essentially no chromatic) coherence.

milestones.title: A laboratory hard X-ray beam produces resolved near-field interference speckles.
milestones.criterion: Resolve near-field speckles produced by a random scattering object under laboratory X-ray illumination. Zanette and colleagues demonstrated this with a liquid-metal-jet source operated at 50 kV and 30 W; mean detected photon energy was approximately 16 keV. One measured profile had 31% visibility. Two specimens were imaged using five 60 s exposures each, with corresponding reference exposures. Published 26 June 2014. The visibility is a reported result, not a universal cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Coherent speckle-imaging community; the laboratory demonstration by the Technical University of Munich, KTH and University College London collaboration.
milestones.threshold_quote: We report on the observation and application of near-field speckles with a laboratory x-ray source.

milestones.title: A laboratory hard X-ray source produces a phase image by far-field ptychography.
milestones.criterion: A hard X-ray beam of photon energy at least 5 keV, generated in a laboratory without a synchrotron or other accelerator facility, is used for far-field ptychography: diffraction patterns from overlapping illuminated regions are reconstructed into an image of the object's phase, and the resolution is measured, for example by Fourier ring correlation between reconstructions from two halves of the data. No flux or acquisition-time threshold applies. Ptychography at a synchrotron detuned to laboratory-source brilliance is partial.
milestones.set_by: Ptychographic imaging community; the test applied in the first laboratory demonstration by the University of Sheffield and Diamond Light Source, 2021.
milestones.threshold_quote: the first proof of concept for far field x-ray ptychography performed using an x-ray laboratory source

milestones.title: A laboratory-scale accelerator drives free-electron-laser amplification in the exponential-gain regime.
milestones.criterion: Radiation from an undulator, a periodic magnet array, is amplified in the exponential-gain regime of a free-electron laser driven by an electron beam from an accelerator of laboratory scale, such as a laser wakefield accelerator, and the gain is measured. Any wavelength counts; the first demonstration was at 27 nm, with about 100-fold gain in the last of three undulators. This shows the amplification mechanism of a compact X-ray laser, not hard X-ray output. Undulator radiation without measured gain is partial.
milestones.set_by: Compact free-electron-laser community; the test applied by Wang and colleagues, Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, Nature 2021.
milestones.threshold_quote: an experimental demonstration of undulator radiation amplification in the exponential-gain regime by using electron beams based on a laser wakefield accelerator

milestones.title: A laboratory-footprint source delivers 10⁶ spatially coherent hard X-ray photons per second.
milestones.criterion: One installation no longer than 50 m, including its driver and shielding, delivers spatially coherent X-rays of photon energy at least 5 keV with measured coherent flux of at least 10⁶ photons s⁻¹ at the sample or through a coherence-defining aperture. This is 1% of the completion flux and 200 times the 5 × 10³ photons s⁻¹ of the first laboratory ptychography. No pulse-rate requirement applies. Total flux without a coherence measurement, or a projected value, is partial.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; an intermediate flux between the first laboratory ptychography and the completion test. No outside body states a coherent-flux ladder.

not_found: No common numerical acceptance test combining laboratory installation size, coherent hard-X-ray flux and photon energy was found.
The full 1996 Nature article could not be opened; its abstract supports the qualitative phase-contrast milestone.
The DARPA Advanced X-ray Integrated Sources announcement (BAA 11-11) could not be opened on 15 November 2026; no numerical target is taken from it.

results.finding: One laser-wakefield-driven free-electron laser demonstrated approximately 100-fold maximum radiation-power gain in its final undulator.
results.detail: Radiation was centred at 27 nm, and measured amplification established operation in the exponential-gain regime. The installation used three undulators; the number of shots used for the gain measurement is not stated.
results.quote: In the third of three undulators in the device, the maximum gain of the radiation power is approximately 100-fold, confirming a successful operation in the exponential-gain regime.

results.finding: Spatially coherent hard X-ray phase-contrast imaging is demonstrated; sample count and numerical coherence or contrast measurements are not reported in the supplied abstract.
results.detail: The abstract reports compatibility with polychromatic microfocus X-ray tubes, but does not explicitly establish that the demonstration used a laboratory source or free-space propagation.
results.quote: Here we describe and demonstrate a simplified scheme for phase-contrast imaging based on an X-ray source having high spatial (but essentially no chromatic) coherence.

results.finding: Laboratory nano-focus X-ray tomography produced propagation-based phase contrast in three test specimens using a source with main emission around 8 keV.
results.detail: Cork, bovine lung and human plaque were imaged with a diverging cone beam and free-space propagation. Phase retrieval improved contrast; no numerical coherence cutoff is required.
results.quote: Further, we have shown that the contrast can be increased by utilising propagation-based phase contrast while retaining the resolution in 3D through incorporation of unsharp masking into the phase-retrieval workflow.

results.finding: Far-field ptychography of one Siemens star test sample reconstructed an object phase image with sub-200 nm resolution.
results.detail: The experiment used 8339 eV synchrotron radiation at Diamond I13-1, with brilliance reported as comparable to liquid-metal-jet laboratory sources. It demonstrates ptychography under laboratory-compatible brilliance, but the X-rays were generated at a synchrotron.
results.quote: The experimental geometry gives a pixel size in real space of 96 nm and the resulting image resolution is sub 200 nm.

results.finding: Laboratory liquid-metal-jet far-field ptychography of one Siemens star produced a phase image with 930 nm resolution.
results.detail: The gallium source supplied 9.25 keV X-rays. Overlapping illumination positions were scanned, and resolution was measured by Fourier ring correlation between reconstructions from two temporal halves of the dataset.
results.quote:
The crossover point of the two curves lies at
1.08 μm−1, corresponding to a resolution of 930 nm, a
factor of more than 5 beyond the spot size at the sample.

results.finding: One laboratory liquid-metal-jet installation measured approximately 5 × 10³ photons s⁻¹ through its coherence-defining pinhole.
results.detail: The beam supported coherent imaging at 9.25 keV, but measured flux was 200 times below the milestone threshold. Source-to-detector distance was 9.4 m; the complete installation footprint including shielding was not reported.
results.quote:
During the experiment, a flux through
the pinhole of ∼5 × 103 photons s−1 was measured.

results.finding: A laboratory liquid-metal-jet source produced propagation-induced edge enhancement in a plastic wedge image at an estimated mean detected energy of 16 keV.
results.detail: The wedge transmission image contains absorption and edge-enhancement signals after free-space propagation. Resolved near-field speckles establish sufficient spatial coherence.
results.quote:
The
transmission image in Fig. 2(a) shows the superposition of
the absorption and the edge-enhancement signals.

results.finding: Laboratory illumination resolved sandpaper-generated near-field speckles; one measured profile had 31% visibility, and two specimens were imaged.
results.detail: The liquid-metal-jet source operated at 50 kV and 30 W; estimated mean detected energy was 16 keV. Each specimen and its reference used five 60 s exposures, averaged before analysis.
results.quote:

results.finding: Laboratory propagation-based phase-contrast imaging of one birch wood skewer improved contrast-to-noise ratio by 5.8×.
results.detail: A rotating molybdenum-anode source operated at 50 kV produced phase fringes after 140 mm of free-space propagation, verified against contact images. No numerical coherence threshold is required.
results.quote:
To apply this technique with the limited x-ray flux available at a
conventional laboratory source, we leverage the contrast enhancement of free-space propagation
phase-contrast imaging, achieving an increase in contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of 5.8x.

results.finding: Laboratory liquid-metal-jet illumination produced resolved near-field speckles; one pixel's scan intensity pattern had 43% visibility.
results.detail: A sandpaper diffuser generated the speckles. Five images at different propagation distances had mean detected energies of 16–21 keV and resolved speckle structures of approximately 56 μm. Speckle scanning also produced phase images of two specimens.
results.quote:
In
Fig. 2(c), the intensity pattern of one random pixel from a scan
is presented with a visibility of 43%.

results.finding: One laboratory XRM-II tungsten-needle scan of a silica-sphere phantom shows propagation phase contrast with a 5 keV lower detection threshold.
results.detail: The nanofocus source produces a polychromatic cone beam without optical elements. Free-space propagation yields residual edge enhancement; Paganin-type phase retrieval is applied to the reconstructed volume. No numerical coherence cutoff is required.
results.quote: Similar to Zeiss X-radia, the XRM-II W-NT scan displays residual phase contrast, most visibly for the bigger spheres.

results.finding: One plastic wedge showed propagation-induced edge enhancement under laboratory illumination with an estimated mean detected photon energy of 16 keV.
results.detail: The wedge transmission image contains a bright edge at the plastic–air interface superimposed on absorption. Free-space propagation produces this contrast; resolved speckles also demonstrate spatial coherence.
results.quote:
The
transmission image in Fig. 2(a) shows the superposition of
the absorption and the edge-enhancement signals.

results.finding: Laboratory liquid-metal-jet illumination resolved sandpaper-generated near-field speckles; one measured profile had 31% visibility, and two specimens were imaged.
results.detail: The source operated at 50 kV and 30 W; estimated mean detected photon energy was 16 keV. Each specimen used five 60 s exposures with corresponding references. Speckles spanned approximately six detector pixels.
results.quote:
The visibility calculated from points A and B is V ¼
ðIA − IBÞ=ðIA þ IBÞ¼ 31%.

results.finding: The Munich Compact Light Source produced propagation-based phase-contrast images of nylon and PMMA phantoms and one ex-vivo mouse at 25 keV; phantom counts were unspecified.
results.detail: The laboratory source supplied partially spatially coherent X-rays. Free-space sample-to-detector propagation produced edge enhancement, and phase retrieval recovered PMMA sphere thickness.
results.quote:
In this report we show that the flux and coherence of the quasi-monochromatic X-ray beam provided by the 
MuCLS allows phase-contrast imaging by simply increasing the sample-to-detector distance.

results.finding: Laboratory far-field ptychography produced phase images of two samples, with 300 nm resolution measured on the Siemens star target.
results.detail: A liquid-metal-jet laboratory source supplied 9.25 keV X-rays. Overlapping scan diffraction patterns were reconstructed with ePIE. Resolution was measured from resolved spoke widths in an azimuthal profile, rather than Fourier ring correlation, which the criterion does not require.
results.quote:

results.finding: One Munich Compact Light Source installation achieved a peak total X-ray flux of 5 × 10¹⁰ photons s⁻¹.
results.detail: The peak was measured at 35 keV and reached only briefly during tuning. The source reports total flux, not measured spatially coherent flux at a sample or through a coherence-defining aperture. The text also does not establish an overall length ≤50 m including driver and shielding.

definition = "An installation that fits in a university laboratory delivers spatially coherent hard X-rays, of photon energy at least 5 keV, with enough coherent flux for the diffraction imaging now done at synchrotron beamlines. Spatial coherence is phase correlation across the beam; coherent flux is the photons per second within the coherent part of the beam.". Reason: Rewritten by Claude Fable 5.2 at the owner's request, 15 November 2026, under the completed-breakthrough standard. The definition asked only for enough coherence for lensless microscopy, with no photon energy, flux or footprint.

edit completion: title = "A laboratory-footprint source delivers 10\u2078 coherent hard X-ray photons per second and a coherent image."; criterion = "One installation no longer than 50 m, including its driver, radiation source and shielding, delivers to a sample spatially coherent X-rays of photon energy at least 5 keV with measured coherent flux of at least 10\u2078 photons s\u207b\u00b9, at a pulse rate of at least 1 kHz or continuously. Photon energy, bandwidth, coherence, flux and pulse rate are measured in one operating configuration, and the footprint is reported. A coherent diffraction measurement made with that beam, such as far-field ptychography, is reconstructed. The results are published after peer review. Any mechanism counts: free-electron laser, inverse Compton scattering, high-harmonic generation or electron impact."; set_by = "Technology Atlas. The 50 m footprint is the UC-XFEL collaboration's design figure for a university-scale X-ray laser; the 5 keV, 10\u2078 photons s\u207b\u00b9 and 1 kHz figures are the Atlas's."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; threshold_quote = "the total longitudinal footprint of the instrument is below 50 m"; threshold_ref = 3; basis = "No agency, programme or standard states a combined footprint, coherence and flux test; DARPA AXiS, NSF CXFEL and UC-XFEL documents were searched. The entry asks for flux sufficient for synchrotron-type measurements. The first laboratory ptychography had about 5 \u00d7 10\u00b3 photons s\u207b\u00b9 through its pinhole and 140 s per scan position, about 7 \u00d7 10\u2075 photons; at 10\u2078 photons s\u207b\u00b9 that exposure takes 7 ms and the 400-position scan about 3 s in place of 16 h. 5 keV is a common lower bound for hard X-rays; 1 kHz is the repetition class the entry names."; refs = [1, 3]. Reason: Rewritten by Claude Fable 5.2 at the owner's request, 15 November 2026, under the completed-breakthrough standard. The test had no scale and was written from the demonstration that met it. It now states photon energy, coherent flux, pulse rate, footprint and the deciding event.

edit m3: title = "A laboratory hard X-ray source produces a phase image by far-field ptychography."; criterion = "A hard X-ray beam of photon energy at least 5 keV, generated in a laboratory without a synchrotron or other accelerator facility, is used for far-field ptychography: diffraction patterns from overlapping illuminated regions are reconstructed into an image of the object's phase, and the resolution is measured, for example by Fourier ring correlation between reconstructions from two halves of the data.
